title: One owned thing: Tämä on …
summary: Identify one owned thing with Tämä on and the already learned owner endings.
objectives: Identify one owned thing with Tämä on and the already learned owner endings.
Apply this rule with the supporting forms shown.

sections.title: How the pattern works
paragraphs: Tämä means “this”, on means “is”: Tämä on identifies one thing. Put the owner phrase after that frame.
Tämä on minun palloni means “This is my ball.” Use the endings already learned: minun (“my”) selects -ni; sinun (“your”) selects -si; hänen (“his”) selects -nsa.
The thing being identified determines on or ovat. Even when several people own one ball, the one-ball frame remains Tämä on. Tasks show whether one person or a group is addressed as “you”.
keyPoints: Identify one owned thing with Tämä on and the already learned owner endings.

steps: Tämä on (“This is”) identifies one thing.
Tämä on (“This is”) identifies one thing.
Tämä on (“This is”) identifies one thing.

commonMistakes: Use on for one thing, regardless of owner number.
Keep the noun ending after the personal owner.

practiceExercises.prompt: Optional practice: Write “This is your apple.” in Finnish. Begin with Tämä on. Address one person. Use omena (“apple”).
practiceExercises.explanation: Tämä on identifies one thing. The ending -si identifies your ownership.

sentenceExplanation.pattern: demonstrative + agreeing olla + optional owner pronoun + possessed noun

parts.formation: Use on with one thing, independently of how many people own it.
Sinun is the personal owner form of sinä; it selects -si.
omena (“apple”) + -si = omenasi. The same possessed form can name one or several things; this sentence names one.

answerDiagnostics.explanation: Drop the noun’s plural -t before -si: use omenasi.
Keep the possessive ending -si even when the owner pronoun is present or omitted.
Sinun needs -si; changing the ending changes the owner.
